title: Catalog: n = p + 2^k (de Polignac / Romanoff / Erdős)
connection: n = p + 2^k (de Polignac / Romanoff / Erdős) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ Σ_k 1/log n ≍ O(1) (log n terms each 1/log n). Obstruction: covering congruences {0 mod 2, 0 mod 3, 1 mod 4, 3 mod 8, 7 mod 12, 23 mod 24} force n−2^k divisible by a small prime. Status: false infinitely often (an AP of odd failures, Erdős 1950); Romanoff: positive lower density of representables. Mechanism: failure = periodic orbit k ↦ 2^k mod m covered by finitely many moduli; density = Romanoff's L¹ bound on r(n).
why: Canonical O(1)-count failure; ES has no periodic witness parameter, so the covering mechanism has no direct ES analogue — the reason why should be stated as a lemma.
first_step: Write the ES witness set at p as orbit(s) of a map and test whether any finite modulus set can 'cover' it; check whether this reproduces B1 sterility.

title: Catalog: n = p + 2^a + 2^b (Crocker)
connection: n = p + 2^a + 2^b (Crocker) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ log n. Obstruction: no single-modulus covering; failures come from an explicit sparse family. Status: false infinitely often (Crocker 1971; Pan 2011 gives ≫ x^{1−ε} odd exceptions ≤ x). Mechanism: an explicit sparse family of odd n (check whether it is built from 2^{2^m}−1 and Fermat-number divisibility, as commonly described).
why: Log-count, no covering, still false i.o. — the sharpest warning that 'log² count + no local obstruction' is not enough; ES's count is log² p.
first_step: Read Crocker 1971 (Pacific J. Math.) and isolate the exact structural input; ask whether an ES analogue (p tied to 2^{2^m}) exists among primes.

title: Catalog: odd n = p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c (Sun's conjecture: every odd n > 8)
connection: odd n = p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c (Sun's conjecture: every odd n > 8) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ log² n — same order as ES. Obstruction: none known. Status: open (conjectured by Z.-W. Sun, arXiv:0901.3075). Mechanism: none; numerics only.
why: Exact twin of ES in expected count (log²) with additive instead of multiplicative witnesses; any proof or disproof calibrates ES directly.
first_step: Check whether Crocker's construction extends to three powers (search 'p+2^a+2^b+2^c exceptions'); compute min witness count / log² n up to 10^9.
refs: arXiv:0901.3075 (Sun, Mixed sums of primes and other terms)

title: Catalog: Sierpiński numbers k·2^n + 1 (78557)
connection: Sierpiński numbers k·2^n + 1 (78557) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ Σ_n 1/(n log 2) = ∞ (divergent, log N up to N) but along a periodic orbit. Obstruction: covering set {3,5,7,13,19,37,73}. Status: false for specific k (covering); smallest Sierpiński number still open (78557 conjectured). Mechanism: covering system on n; also partial algebraic factorisation variants (Filaseta et al.).
why: Shows a divergent expected count can still vanish identically when the parameter is periodic mod the covering moduli.
first_step: Formulate an 'ES-Sierpiński' question: a family p(t) of primes candidates for which every ES certificate line is killed mod fixed primes; relate to T1.

why: Same mechanism as Sierpiński; included for completeness of the covering family.
first_step: Note: ES certificate families are also 'k·m + 1' shapes (4Cp+1): check whether any covering-type identity is impossible for them by B1.

first_step: Check the size of the smallest known Brier number and the covering moduli used.

connection: Erdős–Straus for 4/n with x ≤ y ≤ z and z ≤ n^k bounded exponent ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: count depends on k. Obstruction: —. Status: unknown; ES solutions can have z ≍ n² (Type I). Mechanism: —.

title: Between: does Crocker's construction extend to p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c?
connection: Sun's three-powers conjecture (log² count, same as ES) vs Crocker's two-powers failure (log count). Resolution tells whether log² + no local obstruction can still fail i.o.
why: If a Crocker-type family kills three powers too, the 'log² is safe' heuristic for ES loses its main support; if Crocker provably cannot extend, the reason is a candidate ES lemma.
first_step: Reconstruct Crocker's family; for its members n compute r₃(n) = #{n = p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c} up to n ≈ 2^64 with Miller–Rabin.

title: Between: Are all exceptions of p + 2^a + 2^b structured (Crocker-type) or are there 'random' ones?
connection: Pan proves ≫ x^{1−ε} exceptions; classify numerically the exceptions ≤ 10^9 by whether they lie in algebraic families.
why: If log-count failures are always structured, then ES (log², and failures provably not AP-structured) gains heuristic support.
first_step: Enumerate odd n ≤ 10^8 not of the form p + 2^a + 2^b; test membership in known families; look at residues mod small primes.

title: Between: Schinzel's N_m growth exponent
connection: Pomerance–Weingartner predict N'_m = exp(m^{1/2+o(1)}); proving any upper bound N_m < ∞ for one m ≥ 4 would be ES-strength.
why: Locates ES (m = 4) on a curve; if exceptions at m = 8..15 follow the Poisson model precisely, the model's prediction 'no exceptions for m = 4' is calibrated.
first_step: Fit observed largest exceptions (PW table: m=8: 241; m=12: 12241; m=15: 20521) against exp(c·m^{1/2}) and against (log p)³/m ≈ const.

title: Between: Why is m = 12 so exceptional in the Pomerance–Weingartner table?
connection: m = 12 has 24 exceptions up to 10^12 vs 9 for m = 10 and 13 for m = 13; the count per m should correlate with an arithmetic singular series (structure of (ℤ/m)^× and −1).
why: An 'ES singular series' S(m, n) that predicts the m-dependence would be the right object to bound below at m = 4.
first_step: Compute heuristic expected counts E_m(p) = Σ_{Type I/II shapes} densities for m = 4..15 and correlate with exception counts.

title: Between: Markoff-type surfaces: non-BM Hasse failures explained by reduction theory
connection: Ghosh–Sarnak find infinitely many k with local points but no integral points, beyond Brauer–Manin; mechanism: Vieta-group fundamental domain is small/empty.
why: ES is integral points on an affine cubic surface with no BM obstruction; a non-BM failure mechanism of reduction type is the most plausible disproof shape.
first_step: Ask whether the ES surface has any infinite group of birational automorphisms preserving integral points (analogue of Vieta moves); if not, record the asymmetry.

title: Between: Sums of three cubes: any non-local, non-BM failure?
connection: If some k ≢ ±4 mod 9 provably had no representation, that would be the first integral Hasse failure on a cubic surface without BM — directly ES-relevant.
why: Calibrates the plausibility of ES failing despite no BM.
first_step: Literature check: 'integral points three cubes Hasse principle failure' (Colliot-Thélène–Wittenberg, Siksek).

title: Between: U(n) sporadic list finiteness
connection: U(n) fails at odd squares + {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}; is the sporadic list finite and what governs it?
why: A 'squares + finitely many sporadic' theorem for U(n) would be the ES-adjacent analogue of Rickards–Stange.
first_step: Check whether sporadic values share a factor pattern (105 = 3·5·7, 2961 = 3·987=3·3·7·47 …) and compute class numbers / Legendre symbols to see a governing invariant.

title: Between: ES over rings of integers O_K with total positivity
connection: Define ES_K: 4/ν = 1/ξ + 1/η + 1/ζ with totally positive ξ, η, ζ ∈ O_K. Does it fail for some K (e.g. Q(√2), Q(√5))?
why: If ES_K fails for a real quadratic K, the failing mechanism (units? positivity at two places?) is a candidate obstruction for ES itself; if it holds via the same covering identities, it's a calibration.
first_step: Search ES_K for K = Q(√2), Q(√5) for small totally positive primes ν with a bounded-height search.

title: Between: Smooth-denominator ES
connection: Require x, y, z to be y-smooth (y = (log p)^A). The count drops with A; find the A where failures start.
why: Gives a tunable count family inside ES; the critical A tells how much 'slack' ES has.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10^6 the minimal smoothness bound of the best solution; fit vs log p.

title: Between: ES with a prime denominator
connection: Require one of x, y, z to be prime. Expected count ≈ log² p / log p ≈ log p — a Crocker-scale count inside ES.
why: If ES-with-prime-denominator fails infinitely often in a structured family, the structure is informative; if it holds to 10^9 that is evidence log-count can hold here.
first_step: Search p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^7 for representations 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with z (or x) prime; list failures.

title: Between: ES with the minimal denominator bounded: x ≤ p/4 + p^θ
connection: Linnik-constant analogue: max over p of minimal admissible window.
why: If the minimal x always lies in a short window, ES becomes a bounded search (Π₁ → decidable per p with explicit bound).
first_step: Compute max_{p ≤ 10^9} (x_min(p) − ⌈p/4⌉)/log² p and fit.

title: Between: Explicit (deterministic) thin additive basis with r(n) ≍ log n
connection: Erdős's construction is probabilistic; check whether an explicit construction with r(n) ≍ log n is known (Kolountzakis gave algorithmic constructions; Jain 2024 discusses open aspects).
why: ES = 'a deterministic log²-count system covers every prime'. Whether explicit log-count bases can be certified is the purest derandomisation analogue.
first_step: Check whether explicit/derandomised constructions with r(n) ≍ log n exist (search Kolountzakis 1995; arXiv:2405.08650).

title: Between: Hensley alphabet at critical dimension δ_A = 1/2
connection: Thin-orbit CF problems at exactly the critical exponent have count ≍ polylog — the closest SL₂ analogue of ES₅.
why: Results (or failures) at δ = 1/2 would tell whether polylog-count thin-orbit statements can be pointwise.
first_step: Search literature for 'critical dimension 1/2 Zaremba' and compute denominators covered for an alphabet tuned to δ ≈ 1/2.

title: Between: Goldbach's other conjecture finiteness (p + 2k²)
connection: Are 5777 and 5993 the only failures?
why: Power count; a proof of finiteness would show how sporadic failures are handled when count is power — template for U(n).
first_step: None beyond literature check.

title: Between: Ternary Egyptian for numerators m with all denominators in an AP
connection: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x,y,z ≡ r mod q: local obstructions appear; which (q,r) still look universal?
why: Maps local obstructions vs global failures in a controlled family.
first_step: Compute for q ≤ 12 the residues r for which all n ≤ 10^6 coprime to stuff are solvable.

title: Between: Erdős's log log b terms conjecture
connection: Every a/b with ≪ log log b terms; Vose gives √log b.
why: Uniform bounded-term phenomena for general a; ES is a = 4 with 3 terms.
first_step: Read Vose 1985 and Tenenbaum–Yokota; check whether their methods give O(1) terms for 4/p on a density-one set (known anyway) or something new.

title: Between: Integral points on log K3 surfaces via fibrations (Harpaz)
connection: Harpaz proved integral Hasse/BM results for some log K3 surfaces using fibration methods conditionally on Schinzel-type inputs.
why: The ES affine surface may be log-K3 or log-general-type; Harpaz-type conditional theorems would give conditional ES-type statements.
first_step: Determine the log Kodaira dimension of the ES affine surface (complement of the boundary in the cubic surface) and check whether Harpaz's framework applies.
refs: Harpaz, 'Integral points on conic log K3 surfaces' (check)

title: Between: Positive-proportion vs almost-all for m/n with fixed large m at moderate n
connection: PW show 'mostly false' near exp(m^{1/3}); is there a regime where density is strictly between 0 and 1 provably?
why: A proved intermediate regime would show where the Poisson model is accurate; ES sits in the 'always' regime.
first_step: Read arXiv:2511.16817 for lower bounds on solvable primes.

title: Between: ES with x, y, z pairwise coprime-to-p structure (Type I only / Type II only)
connection: Is every p solvable by Type I alone? by Type II alone?
why: If one type alone fails for some p, ES's robustness depends on two independent mechanisms — an interesting structural fact.
first_step: Compute R_I(p), R_II(p) separately for p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^8; list p with R_I = 0 or R_II = 0.

title: Between: ES restricted to one certificate family per p-class (Mordell-style) with growing modulus
connection: Mordell's covering of non-square classes uses fixed moduli; with growing moduli (one new modulus per scale) does the proportion of uncovered primes go to 0 at a rate?
why: Measures how fast the 'identity' approach degrades; (J)10 growing-level loophole.
first_step: Compute uncovered proportion of primes ≤ x by identities of level ≤ L as L grows.

title: Feature: ES as an infinite covering of primes by arithmetic progressions
connection: Dividing-line feature 'ES as an infinite covering of primes by arithmetic progressions'. ES IS exactly this: ES(p) ⟺ p lies in some AP −f mod 4ad (f | 4a²d+1) or a Type II AP. To supply it one could: study the AP system {−f mod 4ad} as a covering problem: covering theory (Hough's distortion method, Balister et al.) bounds what finite subsystems can do; the infinite system's density Σ 1/φ(4ad)·#f diverges
why: Covering-system technology decides p + 2^k (failure); ES is the dual 'must cover' statement — the same technology might show that an infinite system with divergent density and specific structure covers all primes.
first_step: Search literature for 'infinite covering systems primes divergent sum of reciprocals' and for Hough/Balister lemmas about uncovered sets under divergent density.

title: Feature: two independent witness mechanisms (Type I and Type II)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'two independent witness mechanisms (Type I and Type II)'. ES HAS two (p divides one vs two denominators). To supply it one could: prove they are negatively correlated as failure events (if Type I fails because factors of many 4Cp+1 avoid −1, Type II must succeed) — a 'dichotomy' proof
why: Dichotomy proofs (Siegel-zero dichotomy, Heath-Brown's Artin) convert two weak mechanisms into a pointwise result.
first_step: Compute correlation between R_I(p) and R_II(p) over p ≡ 1 mod 24; negative correlation is a lead.

title: Feature: witness = divisor in a class (multiplicative) rather than prime value (additive)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'witness = divisor in a class (multiplicative) rather than prime value (additive)'. ES HAS multiplicative witnesses; parity barrier is not obviously relevant. To supply it one could: use multiplicative-function machinery (Halász, Matomäki–Radziwiłł) on indicator-type functions of 'has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'
why: Problems with prime-valued witnesses hit the parity barrier; divisor-in-class problems are governed by Stewart-type subgroup criteria instead.
first_step: Express 1[N has a divisor ≡ −1 mod q] in terms of characters of (ℤ/q)^× via the subgroup criterion and check if Halász-type bounds apply when N runs over 4Cp+1, C ≤ X.

title: Feature: exception set closed under a natural operation
connection: Dividing-line feature 'exception set closed under a natural operation'. ES ES exceptions (if any) are closed under nothing obvious; solvable set is closed under multiples. To supply it one could: find an operation T on primes (e.g. p ↦ prime factor of some f(p)) with ES(T(p)) ⇒ ES(p); then descent along T
why: Descent proofs need such operations (Fermat's descent from p | x²+y² to smaller primes).
first_step: Search for identities: 4/p solvable if 4/q solvable for some q | (p + k) with structured k — test numerically which small-q solutions lift.

title: Feature: Linnik-constant bound (smallest witness ≤ n^A)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Linnik-constant bound (smallest witness ≤ n^A)'. ES UNKNOWN for ES; known witnesses are small in practice. To supply it one could: prove a conditional (GRH) bound on the smallest certificate parameter, turning ES into a finite check per p
why: Least-witness theorems (Linnik, Bach) are among the few pointwise polylog results, though conditional.
first_step: Compute max over p ≤ 10^9 of the minimal Type I parameter a·d (or C) and compare with log² p.

title: Feature: height growth / Baker-type forcing
connection: Dividing-line feature 'height growth / Baker-type forcing'. ES LACKS (no linear forms in logarithms appear). To supply it one could: seek a formulation where nonexistence of an ES certificate forces a very good rational approximation or a small linear form in logs, contradicting Baker
why: Primitive divisors (BHV), Catalan-type results use Baker-type lower bounds to force existence of divisors.
first_step: Ask: if every 4Cp+1 (C ≤ X) has all prime factors in a subgroup H_C avoiding −1, is there an associated multiplicative relation among small primes that Baker could forbid?

title: Feature: Galois-theoretic forcing of divisor classes (cyclotomic/Lucas)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Galois-theoretic forcing of divisor classes (cyclotomic/Lucas)'. ES LACKS: ES needs divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C of linear forms, which no cyclotomic structure forces. To supply it one could: use Lucas sequences U_n(P,Q) with discriminant D: primitive divisors r of U_n satisfy r ≡ (D/r) mod n, so negative D gives r ≡ −1 mod n for inert r — choose (P,Q) depending on p
why: Zsigmondy/BHV force divisors in classes ±1 mod n; a −1 mod 4C class appears naturally for inert primes.
first_step: Construct for given p a Lucas sequence whose n-th term equals (or divides) 4Cp+1 or a related ES integer; check whether its primitive divisors can be forced inert.

title: Feature: algebraic factorisation of the auxiliary integer (Aurifeuillian)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'algebraic factorisation of the auxiliary integer (Aurifeuillian)'. ES HAS at squares (T1-type identities) and nowhere else known. To supply it one could: classify all polynomial families of n for which the auxiliary integers 4Cn+1 factor algebraically; each family is a candidate thin exceptional set or a solved family
why: Sierpiński numbers with partial algebraic factorisations and Hardy–Littlewood H at squares show algebraic factorisation is a failure (or success) mechanism.
first_step: For n = m², m³, m²+1, … compute whether 4Cn+1 factors as polynomials in m for some C(m) and whether the factors land in the ES class.

title: Feature: self-reducibility to smaller instances
connection: Dividing-line feature 'self-reducibility to smaller instances'. ES HAS ES(n) ⇐ ES(prime factor) (downward), LACKS upward/sideways reductions among primes. To supply it one could: find 'sibling' implications ES(q) ⇒ ES(p) for q related to p (e.g. q | 4p + 1)
why: Inductive proofs need sideways reductions; four-squares uses n ↦ prime factors and composition.
first_step: Test numerically: is there a rule mapping each p to a smaller prime q with ES(q)'s solution transforming into ES(p)'s? (SIBLING.md)

title: Transfer: ES as a Linnik-type problem in the progression 1 mod 4p
connection: For fixed p the auxiliary integers N_C = 4Cp + 1 run through the AP 1 (mod 4p) indexed by C; ES (Type I) asks for an element N_C with a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C. This is a 'least element of an AP with a factorisation property' question, like Linnik's least prime in an AP.
why: Linnik-type theorems are pointwise in the modulus 4p (power reservoir of AP elements up to (4p)^L) — but the required class mod 4C moves with C, the B2 feature.
first_step: Count, for p ≤ 10^6, the least C with a valid divisor and compare with log² p and with the least prime ≡ 1 mod 4p; check whether 'C ≤ p^ε' always holds.

title: Transfer: trial-count × success-probability profile
connection: Classify thin problems by (#trials, success probability per trial): Goldbach (power, 1/log²), p + 2^k (log, 1/log), ES (C ≤ X gives X trials but success ≈ 1/C-ish ⇒ Σ ≈ log² X).
why: ES has power-many trials but harmonically decaying success: a distinct profile from both 'power reservoir' and 'log trials'. Problems with the same profile and their status would be the right comparison class.
first_step: Find other problems with harmonic success profiles: e.g. 'n has a divisor d ≡ −1 mod k for some k ≤ X' (Stewart-type), and check what's known pointwise.

title: Transfer: Chen-type switching over the C-variable
connection: Sieve the linear sequence N_C = 4Cp + 1 (C ≤ X, p fixed) to make N_C a P₂ = q·r; then ES needs q ≡ −1 mod 4C, equivalently r ≡ −1 mod 4C. Switching principle: count pairs via the other factor.
why: Fixed p, varying C: a one-dimensional linear sieve with level of distribution from Bombieri–Vinogradov-type results for the modulus-varying class condition.
first_step: Write the bilinear form Σ_{C} Σ_{qr = 4Cp+1} 1[q ≡ −1 (4C)] and check which equidistribution input (in q over moduli 4C) is needed.

title: Transfer: Maynard–Tao tuples of C's
connection: Choose C ∈ {C₀h₁, …, C₀h_k} admissible and force many N_{C_i} = 4C_i p + 1 to be almost-prime simultaneously, then use the multiplicative relations between them to force a class −1 factor.
why: Multi-dimensional sieves produce simultaneous structure; ES needs one success among many correlated shifted integers.
first_step: Check whether the N_{C_i} with C_i = C₀h_i (fixed p) form an admissible linear tuple in the variable C₀.

title: Transfer: Type I through binary quadratic forms of discriminant −4d
connection: f | 4a²d + 1 = (2a)²d + 1 means f is primitively represented by a form of discriminant −4d; Type I at (a,d) ⟺ p ≡ −f (mod 4ad) for such f. ES becomes a union of genus/class conditions on p modulo 4ad.
why: Brings class groups and genus theory of Q(√−d) into ES; class-group positivity is a proved-side mechanism.
first_step: For d ≤ 50, compute the set of residues −f mod 4ad realised by represented f, and check how quickly the union over (a,d) covers all classes mod lcm (local covering) vs primes.

title: Transfer: Duke equidistribution for represented values
connection: As d grows, values of forms of discriminant −4d (Heegner-type points) equidistribute (Duke 1988); this might equidistribute the residues −f mod 4ad that Type I offers.
why: Equidistribution in d at fixed p would give many independent chances; pointwise in p requires equidistribution uniform in a small window of d.
first_step: Check the error terms in Duke's theorem vs the window of d needed (d ≤ log^A p).

title: Transfer: Kneser/Olson subset-product theory for gate G4
connection: Stewart's criterion: a fraction fails 2-term representation iff the prime factors of the relevant integer lie in a subgroup H avoiding −1. Kneser/Olson/Davenport-constant bounds describe when subset products must hit −1.
why: ES failure ⟺ for every C, all prime factors of the relevant auxiliary integers lie in subgroups H_C ∌ −1 — a simultaneous confinement over many C.
first_step: Quantify: for random integers N ≡ 1 mod q, the probability of H-confinement ≈ (log N)^{−(1−1/[G:H])}; multiply over independent C to get the heuristic failure rate; compare with data.

title: Transfer: reciprocity across C: simultaneous confinement contradiction
connection: If all prime factors r of N_C lie in H_C ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× for many C, then quadratic reciprocity links (q/r) for q | C to (N_C/q) = (1/q) = 1. Try to derive a contradiction from many C simultaneously.
why: Exactly how T1 arises at squares; at primes, the reciprocity constraints may be insufficient — finding where they stop is informative.
first_step: Recheck MODP_RECIPROCITY.md and TWISTED_T1.md for the multi-C version.

title: Transfer: half-dimensional sieve for confined integers
connection: Integers whose prime factors lie in a subgroup H of (ℤ/q)^× have density ≍ (log x)^{−(1−|H|/φ(q))}; Iwaniec's half-dimensional sieve gives lower bounds for such sets in sequences.
why: ES failure = simultaneous confinement; sieve UPPER bounds for confinement in the C-aspect at fixed p are the pointwise question.
first_step: Formulate the upper-bound sieve problem: #{C ≤ X : N_C is H_C-confined} ≤ ? and see whether the expected X·(log)^{−1/2} type bound is attainable pointwise.

title: Transfer: Heath-Brown's 'one of three' trick for Artin → ES families
connection: Heath-Brown showed one of three multiplicatively independent integers is a primitive root for infinitely many primes using that p − 1 can be made to have few prime factors.
why: An analogous statement 'one of three fixed ES families solves ES(p) for all p in a set S of positive density' could be the first infinite-structured progress.
first_step: Find three ES families whose failure sets intersect only in primes with a special multiplicative structure; test numerically intersection of failures for pairs/triples of small-(a,d) families.

title: Transfer: AGP-style construction for a disproof (many primes failing simultaneously)
connection: AGP build L with many primes q, q−1 | L. Dually, a counterexample search could build p with p ≡ prescribed residues mod many 4ad simultaneously (CRT) — avoiding all Type I APs up to a bound.
why: Covering-type disproofs fail for ES (failures can't fill an AP), but CRT-constructed 'avoiders' up to a bound X show how many families can be dodged simultaneously; prime in the CRT class then by Linnik.
first_step: Compute the density of residue classes mod lcm{4ad : ad ≤ X} avoiding all Type I/II APs; how fast does it decay with X? (Gives an 'avoidance exponent'.)

title: Transfer: Integral Manin heuristics for the ES fibre
connection: For fixed n the ES equation defines an affine cubic surface; integral-point counting conjectures (Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel; Wilsch, Santens for log Fano) predict (log H)^b growth with a product of local densities as constant.
why: Gives a principled 'singular series' for R(n): ES fails only if the leading constant vanishes (T1?) or by fluctuation.
first_step: Compute the log Kodaira dimension / boundary divisor of the ES fibre and check which integral-point conjectures apply; compare predicted exponent b with the observed log² p.

title: Transfer: hyperbolic lattice-point counting in log-size regions
connection: Type II solutions are integer points on a quadric-type variety in a region whose volume grows only like log² p; equidistribution theorems (Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak, Eskin–McMullen) need power-size regions.
why: Explains in a geometric language why ES sits below the 'counting with error term' regime; points to effective equidistribution in small regions as the needed input.
first_step: Identify an explicit quadric Q and region R_p with #(Q(ℤ) ∩ R_p) = R_II(p); compute vol(R_p).

title: Transfer: Serre thin sets and the image of ES integral points
connection: The set of n with ES solutions is the image of integral points of the ES threefold under the projection to n. Hilbert irreducibility says images of covers are thin; ES asks the image to be everything.
why: Positive statements 'image = everything' are proved for maps with sections (identities) — ES has sections on non-square classes only (Mordell–Schinzel).
first_step: Phrase Mordell–Schinzel as 'no section over the square classes' and ask whether a multisection of growing degree (growing-level identities) exists.

title: Transfer: Halász / Matomäki–Radziwiłł for confinement indicators
connection: The indicator that N has all prime factors in H ⊂ (ℤ/q)^× is multiplicative in N; Halász-type theorems give mean values over short intervals / sequences.
why: Pointwise confinement over the sequence N_C (C ≤ X) is a mean of a multiplicative function along an AP 1 mod 4p — Matomäki–Radziwiłł style results along APs may bound it.
first_step: Check whether MR-type results apply to multiplicative functions along APs with modulus as large as 4p and length X ≈ p^θ.

title: Transfer: Smith's method: ES 'spin' distribution
connection: Koymans–Milovic and Smith control 2-power class group ranks via bilinear 'spin' sums. ES's Type I success for fixed (a,d) is a Jacobi-symbol-type condition on p; the joint distribution over many (a,d) might be a spin system.
why: Smith's method proves 100% results when pointwise criteria lack governing fields — exactly ES's apparent situation.
first_step: Check whether the indicator of 'p solved by (a,d)' can be written via Jacobi symbols (p/q) for q | 4a²d+1 and how they interact for different (a,d).

title: Transfer: Heegner points on modular curves X₀(N) with N tied to p
connection: Look for CM points of discriminant −4p or −p (for p ≡ 1 mod 4 one has Q(√−p)) on a curve mapping to the ES surface.
why: Heegner constructions give O(1)-count pointwise existence at every prime in a class.
first_step: Determine whether the ES surface over Q is rational (it is a cubic surface with rational points, so likely rational) and look for curves of genus ≥ 1 in it parametrised modularly.

title: Transfer: Zagier-style involution on I3 words p = tuv − u − v
connection: The I3 reformulation gives a finite set of (t,u,v); look for an involution composed of 'flip' moves (u ↔ v, and a windmill-type move) with a unique fixed point.
why: Windmill involutions prove two squares for p ≡ 1 mod 4 using only a finite set and parity; ES has finite certificate sets too.
first_step: Compute #{(t,u,v): tuv − u − v = p, t,u,v ≥ 1 with coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p)} mod 2 for p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^5.

title: Transfer: Davenport-constant zero-sum forcing for G4
connection: Any sequence of length ≥ D(G) in a finite abelian group has a zero-sum subsequence; analogously, many prime factors in (ℤ/4C)^× force subset products to cover cosets.
why: If N_C has many prime factors (> D((ℤ/4C)^×)), subset products cover a subgroup coset; ES needs −1 in the generated subgroup, not just zero sums.
